problem: Robot task systems usually need rigid input formats and do not combine free-form spoken commands with socially compliant navigation among crowds. Prior LLM planning work such as SayPlan lacks speech input and social navigation controllers.
motivation: Robots in shared human spaces (retail, offices, hospitals) must take natural, varied spoken commands for multi-step pickup-and-delivery tasks. The paper argues an LLM can act as a translation layer that turns free-form commands into a standardized format, so simple regex parsing and off-the-shelf navigators are enough.
key_idea: Use speech-to-text plus Llama3-8B as a translator into a regex-parsable form (pickup location, item, delivery location), then run a finite-state machine over a coordinate dictionary with DRL-VO or Nav2 for navigation.
insight: A small LLM used only as a normalizing translation layer, followed by simple regex parsing, is enough to handle varied commands. The authors report that the larger Llama3 model hallucinated specific room numbers for generic locations, so they chose the 8B model, which could also run onboard. Volunteers found that articles such as 'the' or 'a' confused the parser, so preprocessing remains the weak point. No ablations are reported.
method: Speech-to-text: the Google Speech Recognition API through the Python speech_recognition library, with ambient-noise calibration over the first second.
LLM translation: text is preprocessed (punctuation removal, formatting) and sent to Llama3-8B (llama3-8b-8192) via the Groq API, which rewrites the command into a standardized structured form.
Regex parsing: regular expressions extract L_pickup, L_delivery and item I from the LLM output.
Coordinate dictionary: parsed locations are looked up in a predefined dictionary of known landmark coordinates, so no semantic planning is needed.

Task FSM: a finite-state machine (Idle, Navigating to Pickup, Picking Up, Navigating to Delivery, Delivering) runs the task; hierarchical planners such as GTPyhop or SHOP are suggested for complex tasks.
Navigation: ROS2 Nav2 in static environments; DRL-VO (a CNN policy using lidar, pedestrian maps and goal) in crowds.

setting.backbone: Llama3-8B (frozen, via Groq API) + Google Speech API + DRL-VO (pretrained CNN policy) / ROS2 Nav2
setting.training_data: none for this paper (pretrained Llama3, Google speech, and DRL-VO used off the shelf)
setting.observation: speech/text command; lidar scans, pedestrian maps and known map for navigation
setting.action_space: velocity commands from DRL-VO / Nav2 toward known goal coordinates
setting.simulator: ROS1 simulation with Turtlebot2 (lobby with pedestrians); ROS2 simulation with Turtlebot3 (empty office); Jackal hardware
setting.privileged: predefined map and dictionary of landmark coordinates

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark. The only quantitative result is 84.37% average speech-to-task classification accuracy, self-reported by 10 volunteers on 10 commands each; other results are qualitative demo videos.
results: Average task-classification accuracy was 84.37% (volunteer self-reported, 10 volunteers x 10 commands). In all three integration tests (Turtlebot3 with Nav2, Turtlebot2 with DRL-VO, Jackal hardware with DRL-VO) the robot completed the task, as shown in videos. No baseline comparisons.
limitations: Evaluation is small and qualitative: self-reported accuracy and demo videos, with no baselines or navigation metrics.
Relies on a predefined coordinate dictionary and a single pickup/delivery template; the NLU is sensitive to articles like 'the' or 'a'; no gripper yet.
Only simple single pickup-delivery tasks are handled by the FSM; complex multi-step planning is proposed but not implemented.
